problem_text: Let A, B ∈ ℚ^× be rational numbers. Consider the quaternion ring D_{A,B,ℝ} = {a+bi+cj+dk | a,b,c,d ∈ ℝ} in which i²=A, j²=B, and ij=-ji=k. Show that D_{A,B,ℝ} is either isomorphic to ℍ (Hamilton quaternion) or isomorphic to M₂(ℝ) as ℝ-algebras. (Lean formalization also requires proving ℍ ≇ M₂(ℝ).)
solution_text:
Proof: Embed A, B into ℝ. The classification depends on the signs of A and B.

Case 1 (A<0 and B<0): Write A=-|A|, B=-|B|. Define φ: D_{A,B,ℝ} → ℍ by i↦√|A|·i_ℍ, j↦√|B|·j_ℍ, where i_ℍ, j_ℍ are standard Hamilton quaternion units. Then φ(i)²=|A|·i_ℍ²=|A|·(-1)=-|A|=A, φ(j)²=|B|·j_ℍ²=-|B|=B, and φ(i)φ(j)=√|A|√|B|·i_ℍj_ℍ=√|A|√|B|·k_ℍ=-√|A|√|B|·j_ℍi_ℍ=-φ(j)φ(i). So φ extends to an ℝ-algebra isomorphism D_{A,B,ℝ}≅ℍ.

Case 2 (at least one of A,B>0): WLOG A>0. Define ψ: D_{A,B,ℝ} → M₂(ℝ) by i↦[[√A,0],[0,-√A]], j↦[[0,B],[1,0]]. Then ψ(i)²=A·I, ψ(j)²=B·I, ψ(i)ψ(j)=[[0,B√A],[-√A,0]]=-ψ(j)ψ(i). This extends to an ℝ-algebra isomorphism D_{A,B,ℝ}≅M₂(ℝ).

Non-isomorphism: ℍ is a division ring (every nonzero element a+bi+cj+dk has inverse (a-bi-cj-dk)/(a²+b²+c²+d²)), so it has no zero divisors. But M₂(ℝ) has zero divisors (e.g., E₁₁·E₂₂=0). An ℝ-algebra isomorphism preserves multiplication, so it would map zero divisors to zero divisors. Hence ℍ≇M₂(ℝ).
solution_summary: Classify D_{A,B,ℝ} by signs of A and B: if both negative, rescale basis to get ℍ; if at least one positive, construct explicit matrix representation (generalized Pauli matrices) to get M₂(ℝ). Show ℍ≇M₂(ℝ) via zero divisor invariant.
answer: D_{A,B,ℝ} ≅ ℍ (when both A<0 and B<0) or D_{A,B,ℝ} ≅ M₂(ℝ) (otherwise), and ℍ ≇ M₂(ℝ)

rounds.question: List all possible approaches to classify D_{A,B,ℝ}: what methods could determine which algebra it's isomorphic to?
rounds.expected_answer: Possible approaches: (1) direct construction of isomorphism, (2) universal property of quaternion algebras, (3) tensor product decomposition, (4) sign-based case analysis on A and B, (5) Hilbert symbol computation, (6) checking if the algebra is a division ring.

rounds.question: Try constructing an isomorphism D_{A,B,ℝ} → ℍ directly. What goes wrong?
rounds.expected_answer: If we try i ↦ √|A|·i_ℍ, j ↦ √|B|·j_ℍ, this works when A,B < 0 (since √|A|²·(-1) = -|A| = A). But when A > 0, we'd need i_ℍ² = A > 0, which is impossible since i_ℍ² = -1 in ℍ. So a single construction doesn't work for all cases — we need to split by signs.

rounds.question: Given the sign-based case split, construct an explicit ℝ-algebra isomorphism D_{A,B,ℝ} → M₂(ℝ) for the case where at least one of A,B is positive. What matrices should i and j map to?
rounds.expected_answer: WLOG A > 0. Map i ↦ [[√A, 0], [0, -√A]] and j ↦ [[0, B], [1, 0]]. Then i² = A·I, j² = B·I, and ij = [[0, B√A], [-√A, 0]] = -ji. This extends to an ℝ-algebra isomorphism D_{A,B,ℝ} ≅ M₂(ℝ).

rounds.question: Now address the second part: show that ℍ and M₂(ℝ) are not isomorphic as ℝ-algebras. What invariant distinguishes them?
rounds.expected_answer: ℍ is a division ring: every nonzero element a+bi+cj+dk has inverse (a-bi-cj-dk)/(a²+b²+c²+d²). So ℍ has no zero divisors. But M₂(ℝ) has zero divisors (e.g., E₁₁·E₂₂ = 0). An algebra isomorphism preserves multiplication, so it would preserve zero divisors — contradiction.

rounds.question: Formalize the non-isomorphism argument: why exactly does an algebra isomorphism preserve the zero divisor property?
rounds.expected_answer: If φ: ℍ → M₂(ℝ) is an ℝ-algebra isomorphism, then φ(xy) = φ(x)φ(y) for all x,y. If M₂(ℝ) has zero divisors (XY = 0 with X,Y ≠ 0), then φ⁻¹(X)·φ⁻¹(Y) = φ⁻¹(XY) = φ⁻¹(0) = 0, with φ⁻¹(X), φ⁻¹(Y) ≠ 0. So ℍ would have zero divisors — contradiction.

rounds.expected_answer: The proof has three parts: (1) Case split on signs of A,B — both negative → Case 1, at least one positive → Case 2. (2) Case 1: rescale basis to get ℍ. Case 2: Pauli matrix representation gives M₂(ℝ). (3) ℍ ≇ M₂(ℝ) via zero divisor invariant. This completes the classification: D_{A,B,ℝ} is isomorphic to exactly one of ℍ or M₂(ℝ).
